title: Objects, classes and the C++ basics
subtitle: Model the problem as things that have data and can do things, then let those things talk to each other.

sections.title: Objects and classes
sections.body: An object bundles state (data members) with behaviour (member functions). A class is the blueprint; objects are instances made from it. Programs run by objects sending each other messages (calling methods).

sections.title: The four pillars
sections.body:
PillarMeaning
Encapsulationhide data; expose a small interface
Abstractionshow what, hide how
Inheritancea new class reuses and extends another
Polymorphismone call, different behaviour by object type

questions.prompt: Making a data member private is an example of…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Access only through the public interface.

sections.title: References and pass-by-reference
sections.body: A reference is another name for an existing variable: int &r = x;. As a parameter it lets a function modify the caller’s variable without pointer syntax, and avoids copying large objects (use const T& to forbid changes).

questions.prompt: Passing by reference differs from by value because…

choices.text: The function works on the original variable.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — References and pass-by-reference

sections.title: Overloading and default arguments
sections.body: Functions with the same name but different parameter lists are overloads; the compiler picks by the argument types and count. Return type alone cannot distinguish them. Default arguments (int add(int a, int b = 10)) let a caller omit trailing arguments. (The DSA Lab’s interpreter is a teaching subset and does not resolve overloads or defaults faithfully, so these are explained here rather than run.)

questions.prompt: Can two functions differ only by return type?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The compiler cannot choose from the call alone.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — overload resolution
figures.note: Resolved at compile time from the argument list.

sections.title: Dynamic memory: new and delete
sections.body: new creates an object on the heap and returns its address; delete destroys it. Pair them: every new needs one delete (new[] with delete[]) or memory leaks. Prefer smart pointers (unique_ptr) in modern C++.

worked.why: new int[100] allocates 100 ints of 4 bytes.

questions.prompt: Memory allocated with new int[5] is released by…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Array form pairs with array form.

sections.title: C++ over C
sections.body: C++ adds classes, references, overloading, templates, exceptions, the STL containers (vector, map, string), and stream I/O (cin, cout). Namespaces (std::) prevent name clashes.
